paragraphs.source_en: No matter what sort of fool my master may be, no matter what incurable invalid he is, he is still my master. Even poets say that one should prize the favor of a lord who gives one a single meal; though I am only a cat, I cannot help caring about my master's future. Because my mind was full of sympathy for my master, I ended up neglecting my observation of the washing place. Just then, a sudden clamor of abuse rose from the medicinal bath, and I thought, “So they are quarreling here too?” When I turned to look, there was not an inch of space at the outlet; it was packed with monsters, with hairy legs and hairless legs thrashing together in confusion. It was early autumn, just as the evening sun was about to set, and steam over the washing place rose thickly all the way to the ceiling, so that the disorderly monsters could be seen only dimly. Cries of “Too hot, too hot!” pierced past both my ears and buzzed chaotically inside my head. Among those voices were sharp tones, gloomy tones, and rough tones, all mingling into an indescribable vast sound that filled the bathhouse. It could only be described as a sound of confusion and delirium; there was nothing else to be said of it. I stood there blankly, fascinated by the spectacle, and did not move for a long while. Then the yelling reached a pitch beyond description, and suddenly, from the crowd shoving and pushing for dear life, a huge man rose up. He was a good three inches taller than the other fellows, and moreover he threw back a red face of which one could not tell whether it had grown out of the beard or the beard had grown out of it. In a voice like a cracked gong, he shouted, “Damp it down at once! Damp it down at once! It is too hot! It is too hot!” That voice and that face, towering above the surrounding crowd, made it seem for an instant as if the entire bath belonged to him alone. He was an overman, the overman of whom Nietzsche speaks. He was the great king among demons, the chief of monsters. As I was thinking this, I heard someone behind the bath answer, “Right! I know.” Startled, I quickly turned my gaze that way; in the dim light I could scarcely make things out, but I saw the bath attendant in his vest hurling a great lump of coal into the furnace with all his might. As that lump passed through the furnace door and crackled and popped, half the attendant's face flashed bright; at the same time the brick wall behind the furnace gleamed through the gloom as though it had caught fire. I found it rather uncanny, so I hurriedly jumped down from the window and went home. On the way home I thought: among those naked multitudes who had stripped off haori, drawers, and hakama and were striving to make everyone equal, there still appeared a naked hero. Thus equality is not so easily achieved, even if everyone strips completely naked.

paragraphs.source_en: When I returned home, I found the household as peaceful as ever. My master, freshly out of the bath, was eating supper with his face shining red. As I climbed in by the veranda, my master said, “What a lazy cat! Where can he have been wandering at this hour?” I looked at the dinner tray; though the household was poor, three or four dishes were set out, among them a grilled fish. I do not know what this fish ought to be called; at any rate, it must have been caught around Odaiba yesterday or thereabouts. I have said before that fish are the least prone to illness and the most robust of creatures. But however robust they may be, if they are grilled and boiled like this, they are done for in the end. It is far better, really, to be sickly and just manage to keep breathing. Thinking this, I sat beside the tray and pretended not to see it, while inwardly calculating, “If an opening appears, I shall help myself.” Cats who do not understand this sort of pretense must resign themselves to never tasting delicious fish. My master picked at the fish once or twice with his chopsticks, made a face as though it were not very good, and then set the chopsticks down. His wife, seated opposite him, worked her chopsticks in silence while carefully observing the opening and closing of his upper and lower jaws.
